summary: Notifications can now be delivered by email. Alerts, health events and system notices could already be sent to a webhook, a Telegram chat or an MQTT broker; each of those needs something an organisation has to set up and keep running, while a mailbox is something every organisation already operates, audits and retains. Email is now a delivery destination alongside the others, with its own recipient list, its own subject prefix so a reader covering several sites can tell them apart, its own severity floor, and the same choice about whether the alert image is attached or merely referenced. The mail server itself is configured once for the whole installation rather than once per recipient list, so there is a single place that decides whether this installation talks to a mail server at all, and a single password to change when it changes. Separately, and more consequentially, the fleet control plane could not send anything anywhere at all. It recorded every event, wrote it to its log and pushed it to any browser that happened to be open, and stopped there — so an operator responsible for fifty sites only learned that one had gone dark if they were looking at the screen when it happened, which is rarely the case at three in the morning. The control plane now delivers outbound like the appliances do, by email and also through the webhook and Telegram settings that had been present in its configuration file all along without ever being used. It also gains a button that sends a real test message through the configured mail server, so the mail path can be proved to work before an incident depends on it, rather than after.
compatibility: Nothing is delivered to anyone until an operator switches it on: mail is off by default, every destination is off unless explicitly enabled, and an installation that upgrades onto this build sends exactly what it sent before. No schema change and no migration. On the appliance the mail server settings are seeded from the existing smtp configuration block, so an installation already pointed at an internal relay for password-recovery email does not configure it twice. Two configurations that could never actually deliver are now refused when they are saved rather than when an alert needs them: a mail server username without STARTTLS (the sender will not put a password on an unencrypted connection, so such a relay silently sends nothing), and email delivery with no mail server enabled. A recipient address containing a line break is rejected outright, since it is the shape a mail-header injection takes. When a mail server accepts some recipients and refuses others, the message is delivered to the rest and the refusals are logged, rather than the whole alert failing because one address in a distribution list has gone stale — and that partial delivery is deliberately not retried, so the working addresses are not sent repeat copies of every alert. The shared mail sender also gained support for several recipients, additional headers and file attachments; myidsan's password-recovery email uses the same sender and is unchanged in content, though a subject containing non-Latin characters is now encoded to the mail standard rather than sent raw, which strict mail servers previously mangled or rejected. Alert emails carry the severity, category and source as headers so recipients can file them with mailbox rules, and timestamps are always stated in UTC and labelled as such. Live-benched against a real two-node fleet and a real mail server, 34 checks, covering delivery, the severity floor, the partial-rejection behaviour, both refusals and a node going offline reaching an operator's mailbox; the screens were driven in a real browser in English and Arabic; 34 deliberate faults introduced into the delivery and validation logic were all caught by the tests.
